subject: computer-science
title: ZIMSEC A-Level Computer Science

officialDocument.title: Computer Science Syllabus, Forms 5 - 6, 2015 - 2022 (Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education, Curriculum Development and Technical Services), examined by ZIMSEC at A Level
officialDocument.publisher: Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education (Curriculum Development and Technical Services) / Zimbabwe School Examinations Council (ZIMSEC)

sourceNote: Topic names and their order (1 to 9) are transcribed from the topic list (6.0) of the Ministry's Computer Science Syllabus Forms 5 - 6 (2015 - 2022), whose items are misnumbered 5.1-5.9 in the copy read; sub-topics are the content items of the competency matrix (8.0, rows 8.1-8.15) and the scope-and-sequence chart (7.0), and the form in which each is taught comes from them. The matrix does not number its content items: all sub-topic codes (1.1 to 9.5, P.1, P.2), all objective codes and the Practical skills node are ours. Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase; no syllabus text is reproduced.
notes: Source (read 2026-10-10): Ministry document, copy obtained from zimsake.co.zw softidrive (the zimsake.co.zw document library; the URL recorded is the library's address because the file has no stable direct link). The cover prints 'Computer Science Syllabus, Forms 5 - 6, 2015 - 2022' (Curriculum Development and Technical Services, Mount Pleasant, Harare; the title is misspelt on the cover and header of the copy read). It was read through a pdftotext rendering in which the scope-and-sequence and competency-matrix tables come out with columns interleaved; check every heading, the form of each item and each objective against a clean copy from ZIMSEC.
Subject code: not printed in the syllabus document. ZIMSEC A-Level Computer Science is commonly cited as 6023 (to be confirmed by the owner); left null.

Heritage-Based Curriculum: ZIMSEC introduced Heritage-Based Curriculum syllabi, and 2024-2030 versions exist for Forms 5-6 in some subjects. Confirm which Computer Science syllabus November 2026 and later A-Level candidates sit, set effectiveTo, and create a new version file when a new syllabus replaces this one. Version dates assumed: first examined in November 2018 (effectiveFrom 2018-01-01).

Numbering: the topic list prints the nine topics as 5.1-5.9 (a misnumbering), the scope and sequence as 7.1-7.9, and the competency matrix as 8.1-8.9 (Form 5) and 8.10-8.15 (Form 6: networking, algorithm design and data structures, programming, computer architecture, software development, security and ethics). This tree follows the topic list order (1-9).

Placement of Form 6 items: the matrix gives Form 6 the cloud service models and types (networking), binary trees, primitive data types and recursion (algorithm design and data structures), object-oriented programming and advanced programming (mobile applications, gaming), software architecture, object-oriented methodology and prototyping, security policies, laws and computer crime, environmental laws and issues, impact of social media and ethical principles. The scope-and-sequence chart also lists, for Form 6 enterprising, e-commerce, telecommunications and business and enterprise, but the matrix has no Form 6 enterprising row; they are treated as part of the Enterprising topic's concepts.

Concepts with no ZIMSEC node because the syllabus assumes them from O Level or does not mention them: LAN and WAN models, topologies, transmission media, internet hardware (Cambridge 2.1), input and output devices, storage and memory types, graphics, sound and compression (Cambridge 1.2-1.3), operating systems and translators (Cambridge 5, 16), assembly language and bit manipulation, Boolean algebra and Karnaugh maps, adders and flip-flops, parallel processing and virtual machines, validation and verification, AI, abstract data types beyond the introduction, OOP in depth beyond the four features, declarative programming and exception handling. They are Cambridge only.

Assessment (9.0) as read: continuous assessment 30% (Paper 3 coursework 10%, Paper 4 project 20%) and a summative examination 70%: Paper 1 free-response theory (3 hours, 100 marks, 30%, 10 to 12 compulsory questions) and Paper 2 practical (3 hours, 100 marks, 40%, 3 sections with 6 practical questions, candidates answer 1 question from each section). Paper 3 coursework (5 terms, 100 marks, 10%): 7 items, five practical assignments and two theory tests (one in Form 5, one in Form 6), set and marked by teachers and moderated. Paper 4 project (4 terms, 100 marks, 20%) from term 2 of Form 5 to the end of term 2 of Form 6, up to 50 pages, marked in five sections A to E (25, 25, 25, 15 and 10 marks).

Specification grid as read (9.3): Paper 1 content distribution Data Representation 15, Networking 20, Computer Architecture 20, Security and Ethics 10, Algorithm Design and Data Structures 15, Databases 10, Enterprising 10 (total 100); the grid has no rows for the SDLC and Programming topics. Paper 2 sections: Computer Architecture 30, Programming, Algorithm design and Databases 40, Networking 30. Skills distribution: Paper 1 knowledge and understanding 30%, problem solving 50%, practical skills 20%; Paper 2 10%, 40% and 50%. The text above the skills table says theory tests are 40% knowledge and 60% problem solving, which does not match the table; confirm against a clean copy.

Practical language: the syllabus names VB.Net, Java and Python among suggested tools and examines the programming language syntax in the project report. This product's practical language is Python; pseudocode follows the Cambridge 9618 pseudocode style for algorithms. Paper 2 (practical) and the project are done on a computer: written practice items test the same skills but cannot replace practice on a machine.

Many concepts are shared with Cambridge 9618 (concepts acs.*). Lessons are written to the depth of the deeper board; parts named only by ZIMSEC (octal, EBCDIC, passive and active electronic components, the OSI model, RIP and OSPF, quick sort, mobile applications, SDLC, software architecture, enterprising, e-waste and the 3Rs) are marked as ZIMSEC detail.
overview: The ZIMSEC A-Level Computer Science syllabus (Forms 5-6) has nine topics. Form 5 covers data representation (number bases, floating point, arithmetic errors, character sets), networking (OSI and TCP/IP models, IP addressing, DNS, routing protocols), hardware architecture (electronics, Von Neumann and Harvard architectures, buses, logic gates, the fetch-decode-execute cycle, addressing modes), security and ethics, the waterfall SDLC, algorithms and data structures (pseudocode, trace tables, sorting and searching), structured programming with arrays and files, databases (relational modelling, normalisation to second normal form, SQL) and enterprising. Form 6 adds cloud computing, software architecture, prototyping and object-oriented methodology, binary trees, recursion, object-oriented programming, mobile applications and games, security policies, laws and computer crime and environmental issues.
assessmentOverview: Continuous assessment carries 30%: coursework of five practical assignments and two theory tests (10%) and a project report (20%). The examination carries 70%: Paper 1 theory with 10 to 12 compulsory questions (3 hours, 100 marks, 30%) and Paper 2 practical with one question from each of three sections (3 hours, 100 marks, 40%).

components.name: Paper 1: Theory (free response)
components.description: 10 to 12 compulsory questions on the whole syllabus; content distribution: Data Representation 15, Networking 20, Computer Architecture 20, Security and Ethics 10, Algorithm Design and Data Structures 15, Databases 10, Enterprising 10.

components.name: Paper 2: Practical
components.description: Three sections (Computer Architecture 30; Programming, Algorithm design and Databases 40; Networking 30) with six practical questions in all; candidates answer one question from each section.

components.name: Paper 3: Coursework
components.description: Continuous assessment over 5 terms: five practical assignments and two theory tests, set and marked by teachers and moderated by ZIMSEC.

components.name: Paper 4: Project
components.description: A project report (up to 50 pages) over 4 terms, marked in five sections: selection, investigation and analysis; design; software development; testing and evaluation; general expectations.

children.name: Number bases
children.description: Binary, octal, denary, hexadecimal and two's complement; the matrix also asks for multiplication and division of binary numbers.

objectives.text: Convert numbers between binary, octal, denary and hexadecimal.
Represent negative integers in two's complement and add and subtract binary numbers.
Multiply and divide binary numbers.
Convert floating-point binary numbers to denary and back.
Normalise floating-point binary numbers and explain why this is done.
Distinguish overflow from underflow and say when each arises.
Interpret arithmetic errors and explain their effect on results.

children.name: Data representation: character sets
children.description: Character sets ASCII, Unicode, BCD and EBCDIC. BCD encoding is taught with the number systems (concept acs.data.number-bases).

objectives.text: Represent data using the ASCII, Unicode, BCD and EBCDIC character sets.
Convert text to binary codes using a character set.

topics.name: Networking
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.2) and Form 6 (8.10). Paper 1 weighting 20%; Paper 2 section (Networking) 30%.

objectives.text: Describe the layers of the OSI and TCP/IP models and map one to the other.
Explain the format of an IP address.
Distinguish between public and private IP addresses.
Explain the role of the Domain Name System.
Describe the Routing Information Protocol (RIP) and Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) and what each is used for.

children.name: Cloud service models and cloud types
children.description: Form 6 (competency matrix 8.10).

objectives.text: Differentiate the cloud service models (SaaS, PaaS).
Describe public and private cloud types and compare them.

topics.name: Computer Architecture
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.3, hardware architecture) and Form 6 (8.13, software architecture). Paper 1 weighting 20%; Paper 2 section (Computer Architecture) 30%.

children.name: Basic electronics: passive and active components

objectives.text: Explain the principle of operation of passive and active electronic components.
Test and replace electronic components.

children.name: Von Neumann and Harvard architecture and processor components

objectives.text: Describe the Von Neumann and Harvard architectures and distinguish them.

Describe the functions of the control unit, the ALU and the registers (program counter, memory data register, memory address register, index register, current instruction register, status register, accumulator).
Explain the use of the control, address and data buses.

children.name: Logic gates
children.description: NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR (with NOT, AND and OR assumed); truth tables of up to three inputs.

objectives.text: Use logic gates, including NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR, to design logic circuits.
Construct truth tables with up to three inputs and calculate the output of a circuit for given inputs.

children.name: Processor speed and pipelining
children.description: Pipelining is named in the syllabus; the RISC and CISC comparison is Cambridge detail within the shared concept.

objectives.text: Identify the factors that affect processor speed and ways of improving performance.
Explain the importance of pipelining.
Describe the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
Identify the types of interrupt (internal, external and software) and justify why computers use interrupts.
Explain the direct, indirect, immediate, indexed and relative addressing modes.

children.name: Software architecture
children.description: Form 6 (competency matrix 8.13).

objectives.text: Construct an architectural design for a given scenario from user requirements.

topics.name: Security and Ethics
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.4) and Form 6 (8.15). Paper 1 weighting 10%.

objectives.text: Explain the difference between data privacy and data integrity.
Analyse common threats and vulnerabilities of computer systems and identify their sources.
Evaluate the main counter-measures to software and system attacks.

children.name: Protection, access control and authentication of data

objectives.text: Evaluate the tools used to eliminate vulnerabilities (anti-virus, firewalls, anti-spyware).
Carry out security administration tasks such as creating accounts and setting permissions.

children.name: Keeping data safe in storage and transmission
children.description: From the objective 'describe how data is kept safe during storage and transmission' (encryption tools); code ours.

objectives.text: Describe how data is kept safe during storage and transmission, including encryption.

children.name: Legislation on computer security and crimes; laws and computer crime
children.description: Form 5 legislation (8.4) and Form 6 laws and computer crime: types and control measures (8.15).

objectives.text: Identify the ICT legislative and regulatory frameworks relevant to security and computer crime.
Describe the types of computer crime and the control measures for each.

children.name: Risk management, disaster recovery and security policies
children.description: Disaster recovery methods and risk management techniques (Form 5, 8.4); security policies (Form 6, 8.15). The matrix also asks for the importance of securing data off-site (cloud computing).

objectives.text: Identify risks to computer systems and explore techniques and practices of risk management.
Formulate a disaster recovery plan for a system failure and outline the importance of securing data off site.
Discuss the purpose of a security policy.

children.name: Code of ethics and business ethics
children.description: Code of ethics at the workplace; business ethics such as fairness, firmness, honesty, self-motivation and integrity (unhu/ubuntu/vumunhu); ethical principles and the ethical impact of existing and emerging technologies (Form 6).

objectives.text: Identify the code of ethics and professional practices in the computing field.
Demonstrate ethical practice in computer science and explain the attributes of business ethics.
Analyse the ethical impact of existing and emerging technologies.

children.name: Impact of social media; environmental laws and issues
children.description: Impact of social media (Forms 5 and 6); environmental laws and issues, e-waste management and the 3Rs (Form 6).

objectives.text: Discuss the dangers and ills of misuse of social media.
Identify the environmental impact of computer use and disposal and describe e-waste management (recycle, reuse, reduce).

topics.name: Systems Development Life Cycle (SDLC)
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.5, software development, waterfall model) and Form 6 (8.14, object-oriented methodology and prototyping). No share of Paper 1 is printed for this topic in the specification grid.

children.name: SDLC: the waterfall model
children.description: Stages: preliminary investigation, feasibility study, system analysis, system design, system development, testing, implementation, maintenance and evaluation.

objectives.text: Identify the opportunity for software development.
Apply the stages of the SDLC (waterfall model) in software development.

children.name: Preliminary investigation, fact finding and feasibility study

objectives.text: Outline fact-finding techniques.
Carry out a feasibility study.

children.name: System analysis, design, development, implementation and documentation
children.description: Also carries testing, maintenance and evaluation of the waterfall stages.

objectives.text: Produce documentation for each stage.
Test, implement, maintain and evaluate a system and present a group project.

children.name: Object-oriented methodology and prototyping
children.description: Form 6 (competency matrix 8.14).

objectives.text: Explain the concept of software process models.
Develop a project using process models such as prototyping.

topics.name: Algorithm Design and Data Structures
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.6) and Form 6 (8.11). Paper 1 weighting 15%; part of the Paper 2 section Programming, Algorithm design and Databases (40%).

objectives.text: Design algorithms for a given situation using sequence, selection and iteration in pseudocode.
Analyse algorithms for a given situation by formulating trace tables.

children.name: Standard algorithms: sorting (bubble sort, quick sort) and linear search

objectives.text: Use bubble sort and quick sort and linear search to solve problems.

children.name: Standard algorithms: binary search
children.description: Binary search is named by the syllabus; insertion sort is Cambridge detail within the shared concept.

objectives.text: Use a binary search to solve problems and compare it with a linear search.
Distinguish between dynamic (binary tree) and static (array) data structures.

children.name: Binary trees and array operations
children.description: Form 6 (competency matrix 8.11): sorting, deletion, insertion and searching in binary trees and arrays.

objectives.text: Perform insertion, deletion, searching and sorting operations on binary trees and arrays.
Outline the primitive data types: integer, floating point, character and Boolean.
Use examples to demonstrate recursion and write algorithms for recursive functions.

topics.name: Programming
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.7) and Form 6 (8.12). Part of the Paper 2 section Programming, Algorithm design and Databases (40%); Paper 1 questions on programming sit within Algorithm Design and Data Structures.

children.name: Types of high-level languages
children.description: Imperative or procedural, declarative, general purpose, special purpose and object oriented.

objectives.text: Describe the features of high-level languages and their types.

children.name: Programming language features
children.description: Constants, variables (local and global), expressions, statements, control structures and block structure.

objectives.text: Use constants, variables, expressions, statements and control structures in a program.

children.name: Structured programming: iteration, multiple selection and nested loops
children.description: Nested loops up to three levels.

objectives.text: Use programming constructs (iteration, multiple selection, nested loops) in structured programming.

children.name: Functions and procedures
children.description: Parameter passing by value and by reference.

objectives.text: Develop programs using functions and procedures with parameters passed by value and by reference.
Manipulate one- and two-dimensional arrays in a program.
Read from and write to a file.

children.name: Interface design: user profiling, input and output design

objectives.text: Design input and output interfaces for a user profile.

children.name: Object-oriented programming
children.description: Form 6 (competency matrix 8.12): classes, encapsulation, polymorphism and inheritance; the matrix also mentions implementing classes and demonstrating a singleton.

objectives.text: Outline the features of object-oriented programming.
Implement classes using encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.

children.name: Advanced programming: mobile applications and gaming

objectives.text: Design games and mobile applications, including ones with an indigenous orientation.

topics.name: Databases
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.8). Paper 1 weighting 10%; part of the Paper 2 section Programming, Algorithm design and Databases (40%).

objectives.text: Describe the characteristics of the file-based approach and its limitations.
Describe the features of a relational database that address those limitations.

children.name: Database management systems
children.description: Features of a DBMS, including the data definition language (DDL) and data manipulation language (DML).

objectives.text: Outline the features of a DBMS.
Write SQL commands to create tables and to query or modify data.

children.name: Relational database modelling: analysis and normalisation
children.description: Normalisation up to second normal form is required by the syllabus.

objectives.text: Design database applications using entity-relationship diagrams (ERDs) and convert ERDs to a relational schema in standard normal form.
Normalise database tables up to second normal form.

children.name: Database management: interfaces and access from a high-level language

objectives.text: Develop interfaces and queries using DBMS tools.
Access data in a database through a high-level language.

topics.name: Enterprising
topics.description: Form 5 (competency matrix 8.9); the scope-and-sequence chart lists e-commerce, telecommunications and business and enterprise for Form 6 with no matching matrix row in the copy read. Paper 1 weighting 10%.

children.name: Application areas of computer science and global trend analysis
children.description: Engineering, research and development, agricultural mechanisation, e-learning and telecommunications; analysis of global trends in computing.

objectives.text: Identify areas where computer science is applied.
Analyse global trends in the field of computing.
Evaluate the importance of e-business, including financial literacy for an ICT business.
Explain the elements of marketing, including the 4Ps, and business strategies, skills and techniques.
Design an ICT-related business proposal.

children.name: Intellectual property rights
children.description: Patents and trademarks; plagiarism and copyright.

objectives.text: Describe the role of intellectual property rights, including patents, trademarks, plagiarism and copyright.

topics.name: Practical skills and project
topics.description: Not a topic of the syllabus: our grouping of the practical assessment (Paper 2), coursework (Paper 3) and project (Paper 4) of section 9.

objectives.text: Design, develop and document computer solutions to a problem using a prescribed programming package.
Clarify source code through comments and structure it with procedures and functions.
Design, run and document tests, using standard, extreme and abnormal data.
Select, investigate and analyse a real problem in the candidate's environment (Section A).
Design the solution, develop it and document it, then test and evaluate it (Sections B to D).
Produce a well-organised report that meets the general expectations (Section E).
